title: Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties
full_review:
As far as summer family films go, "Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties" (20th Century Fox) represents, to paraphrase the Dickens classic from which the title playfully borrows its name, the best of trends and the worst of trends: unobjectionable yet uninspired, visually competent yet narratively anemic.

Trivial albeit innocuously entertaining, the film is a sequel to the 2004 comedy based on characters from the long-running Jim Davis comic strip about a wisecracking, lazy orange housecat, here once again computer animated and lethargically voiced by Bill Murray.

This time, Garfield and pooch pal Odie travel to England, stowing away in the luggage of their owner, Jon (a returning Breckin Meyer), who crosses the pond to propose to his veterinarian girlfriend, Liz (played as before by Jennifer Love Hewitt).

Once there, Garfield inadvertently switches places with a royally pampered, identical feline, Prince (voiced by Tim Curry), who has just inherited a castle, finding himself in the treacherous cross hairs of the estate's kitty-hating, next-in-line human heir, Lord Dargis (Billy Connolly).

Directed by Tim Hill, the follow-up improves on the first with writing slightly more clever and the two-legged actors (Meyer and Hewitt) getting less screen time. This leaves more time for the cartoon cat to interact with the manor's menagerie, voiced by the likes of Bob Hoskins, Vinnie Jones and Rhys Ifans, highlighted by a funny kitchen scene in which Garfield instructs the barnyard staff in the art of lasagna-making. There is quite a bit of belching, and Lord Dargis suffers repeated strategically placed dog bites imperiling the continuation of the royal bloodline, but most of the jokes are harmless.

Still, while the prince and pauper plot provides more story, the bland script once again relies heavily on the kind of screwball sight gags and slapstick that the kiddies may find amusing, but -- even at a mere 75 minutes -- may induce accompanying adults to take a catnap.

The film contains some mildly crude humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.
